study.title: Psalms 78 The memory of grace, the rebelliousness of the people and the choice of David
study.overview: This psalm is a long lesson in sacred history in the form of instruction. Asaph calls the people to hear, remembers the mighty works of the Lord in the exodus and in the wilderness, exposes the persistent unbelief of Israel, and shows that even so God acted with mercy, judgment, and faithfulness to his purpose. The movement of the psalm goes from memory to warning and, finally, to the choice of Judah and David as a shepherd of the people. The central teaching is that the present generation must learn from the past to trust in God, obey him from his heart and not repeat the hardness of the ancestors.

outline.title: Called listening and duty to transmit faith
outline.explanation: Asaph opens the psalm as a solemn instruction. He does not just want to inform, but to form the people: the works of the Lord must be taught to the children so that the next generation puts his hope in God, do not forget his deeds and keep his commandments. The contrast is with rebellious parents, unstable heart and unfaithful spirit.

outline.title: Rebellion of Ephraim, deliverances in the wilderness and provision despite unbelief
outline.explanation: The psalm recalls a shameful defeat of Ephraim and then travels through the acts of God in Egypt and in the wilderness: opening the sea, guide of the cloud and fire, water of the rock, manna, and quails. He then denounces the murmuring of the people, who doubted God's ability to supply bread and flesh. Even so, the Lord showed just anger against unbelief, but also compassion, saving them by remembering that they were fragile as flesh and wind.

outline.title: Persistence of sin, plagues in Egypt, and discipline over Israel
outline.explanation: The second great warning shows the repeated cycle of rebellion and forgetfulness: the people provoked God in the wilderness and did not remember his mighty hand. The psalm revisits the plagues of Egypt and the liberation of the people, but then describes Israel's in the promised land, including idolatry in pagan altars. The consequence was harsh: Shiloh's rejection, loss of the ark, military defeat and humiliation of enemies, as a response to God's offended holiness.

outline.title: The Choice of Judah, Zion, and David
outline.explanation: At the conclusion, God rejects the tent of Joseph and the tribe of Ephraim, but chooses Judah, mount Zion and his servant David. The king shepherd comes from the loves to shepherd Jacob and Israel with an upright heart and skillful hands. The end of the psalm shows that the history of judgment does not end in abandonment, but in government chosen by God and pastoral care for his people.

study.context: The psalm attributed to Asaph has a form of instruction for the community. The notes treat him as a historical and sapiential psalm, whose goal is to teach the present generation through the memory of the acts of God and the sins of Israel. The clearest biblical backdrop, according to the notes, includes the exodus, the crossing of the sea, the provision in the desert, the rebellion in the period of pilgrimage and the memory of the defeat linked to the ark in ancient times. There is also reference to David's later choice as a king-grandmother.
study.theology: The Psalm teaches that the memory of God's works is an essential part of the faithfulness of the people. Forgeting the Lord is not mere intellectual failure; it is a spiritual posture that produces rebellion, murmuring and idolatry. At the same time, the text highlights two truths that go together: the holiness of God, who responds to sin with anger and discipline, and his mercy, which sustains the people despite their infidelity. The provision in the wilderness reveals abundant grace, but does not confirm unbelief; but rather makes sin more serious. In the end, the choice of Judah, Zion and David shows that God rules history according to his will, rejecting human self-reliance and raising a shepherd according to his purpose. In evangelical Christian language, the psalm also prepares the heart to wait in God and to recognize what true leadership comes from the Lord Himself, not from human strength.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm presents the history of Israel in the form of parable to teach wisdom; the teaching is not mere account, but a call to spiritual understanding.
The initial verses show that psalm is an instruction for the church: if we do not receive the teaching, the fault is not in the text, but in our willingness to hear it.
The expression translated as a parable can also mean numerous examples; thus, the psalm teaches through concrete episodes of the history of the people.

questions: What concrete practices does our family or community use to remind and transmit to the next generations the works of God?
In which areas do I, like Israel in the wilderness, have I tested God instead of trusting in his salvation?
How does David's choice as a pastor challenge our idea of leadership: more appearance and power, or integrityful heart and service?
study.practice: Read this psalm as a community-conscious examination. Set up time to tell the youngest a specific work that God has done in his life or in church history, using simple and faithful language. Then identify a complaint, fear, or habit of oblivion that has weakened your trust in God. Confess this in prayer and replace the murmuring with gratitude and practical obedience. If you exercise any leadership, take David as a contrast: seek to guide with sincerity of heart, skill in service, and submission to the will of God.
study.uncertainty: The scores provided do not accurately identify the historical episode of 78:9 and suggest the defeat of Ephraim's children in connection with Eli's days; therefore, this relationship should be treated with caution. It is also not possible to state, based only on notes, additional date details, composition or exact circumstances of the psalm. Where the notes differ in emphasis, they were presented as interpretations, not as absolute conclusions.
